evidence.quote: Yeah, we have this arm of our business we call LUMA. It's one of our services offerings now that we're part of this organization, really going through LUMA practitioner training. Something we try to break away from is people thinking they're not a designer. If you've put together a slide deck, if you've done a drawing, and everybody drew when they were a kid, you're a designer at heart. So everybody actually needs to embrace the fact that they are a designer. You may not do it by trade, and you may not do it to the proficiency of those in the design community, but everybody can design, and there are tools out there that can help you. The point is that visual pictures, whether it's a customer journey map, a diagram, or even a data analytics diagram, let you absorb information faster than if you were to read a document. It's that visual element of being able to contextualize information much quicker that really speeds up your ideation process, speeds up how you make decisions, what you decide to take to market. Now that I work at Mural and I do that more frequently than I did previously, I can see how we can get to the disagreements faster. How do we get to where the challenges and bottlenecks are so much faster when it's visual? Leading by Example: Everybody Should Be Shipping
evidence.speaker: Elaina O'Mahoney

evidence.quote: Yeah, it's also something we went through here at Mural, which hopefully is relevant to other product leaders and to engineering, design, and product teams. He is so good here. He's automated 50% of our processes already." And when I think back, it's actually probably better that he's there automating a different part of our business than me stealing him for us. But he's able to showcase his work in Mural. He shares it with the entire organization, and it gives people these lightbulb moments in every department. Tapping the Community Without Chasing ROI
evidence.speaker: Elaina O'Mahoney

evidence.quote: One of the things I think is unique about your product is the community aspect. Some companies have decided to open source their product or tap into communities, which is easy to say and hard to crack, because this is not just a discussion forum where people propose ideas. evidence.speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia

evidence.quote: Yeah, we've actually introduced a newer community within Mural, and we've got a subset of our customers who are first invited to it. evidence.quote: I think the first thing comes with measurement, which was actually the first inclination of most organizations: "Here's a tool, just use it." So it's really about starting with a measurement layer, and then measuring how they're using it. Just because you can with AI, and I'm probably going to say the controversial thing, doesn't mean you need to do it with AI. Maybe spell check with AI is quite expensive. There are other things that can do spell check that don't have AI. So can we apply it to the right things? Can we at least measure our costs? Everything is going to come back to learning loops at the moment, that give us the flexibility of decision-making and don't go too far down the future casting of decision-making, because it's really hard to pull back pricing models. Once pricing models are in the air, people are really going to fight tooth and nail to not change them. And the last thing we're trying to make sure of is predictability. Any business has to understand its cost when things are so uncertain. So the cost of our tool can't wildly swing from month to month at all. There has to be predictability to it, so they can continue investing, so it can incentivize the right usage behavior, and people can get value out of it freely. How Mural Structures Its Product Teams
evidence.speaker: Elaina O'Mahoney

Susie, can I siphon some of your tokens?" And now it disincentivizes the wrong behavior. So it's a decision we're taking with the utmost care. We have to think of pricing models throughout that same range, and maybe the pricing models are completely different. You also have issue-tracking tools like Jira or Linear trying to communicate, "This is the place where work gets done." But the reality is it's still unclear where work gets done, where agents are being deployed, as companies try to truly deploy this in a way that drives adoption. It's not just a few people creating their own context. Where does work happen, and how does the right flow of information have to go?
evidence.speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia

evidence.quote: Yeah, it's an interesting concept, where every tool right now in the stack is almost converging in a circular area, and everybody is also converging on a chat-widget UI where work happens. How many different companies have the same tagline of "where work happens"? OKRs can be in a certain area, and it'll say what work is planned, and then you can measure against what's been planned. Slack is very good for communication in the moment. Then you'll have Notion, Confluence, Docs, Jira, or Linear, where you're still planning work or capturing decisions that have been made. The space that really is still ambiguous is how decisions are getting made and the context of why. That's a blank canvas area we think we're converging on. Yes, in meetings we talk about stuff, but the meeting notes come after; they capture a summary. You still don't have the context of why the decision was made. So how do you bring some of this disparate information together and really get to the why behind decision-making in the moment? When AI Is a Layer, Not a Button
evidence.speaker: Elaina O'Mahoney

evidence.quote: Your product has both angles. You have the consumer, or the employees, or the smaller businesses, as well as large enterprises. In a small-scale business, you have no choice; you have to do a lot of different things. But when you start talking about very large companies, over a thousand employees, maybe they use your product in a known way, for brainstorming and things like that. How do you go about highlighting the new horizon, and making sure that people who are not super technical yet feel comfortable and get that feeling of magic? Creating a Safe Space to Try and Fail Elaina O'Mahoney | Mural 00:14:42 Yeah, I think it's actually lowering the bar for somebody to learn in a lower-risk environment. What AI has created is almost the haves, where you have to virtue signal that you're always ahead of the game, on the frontier, versus those who are like, "I think I can write my emails and do the summaries, and I can even write a Slack bot that summarizes the things I need to do in the morning." But how do you give them the space to showcase what they're doing and ask, "Am I on the right track?" Or somebody who's doing something very frontier and proficient: are you creating the space for them to just try? Because AI is so solo-player mode, it's really hard to see people work out in public and get ideas for how to move forward. So when you're working for Fortune 500 companies, how do you create a safe space that gets more people to try things, but fail at first when trying? I mean, Carlos, I'm sure you tried to write many different things over and over again, and you had to learn by failing with a lot of these tools. How do you create that same environment for employees?
evidence.speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia

evidence.quote: Yeah, it can serve multiple purposes. A community that inspired me earlier on was Lenny's community. If you're just trying out the tool, they'll invite you to the Slack community, and it's there that everything is about adapting to change, doing something brand new. When you're doing something brand new and there isn't a playbook to follow, that's when community is most important. It's creating this trusting, open environment where people can say, "I've tested this out, I've done it this way," or you can ask a more vulnerable question, and people are there to almost say, "I know an answer, I've tried it this way," or "I can connect you with somebody else. Do you want me to show you?" It's the value of that loop that's actually quicker, because you're getting it from people not inside your echo chamber. The Black Market for Tokens
evidence.speaker: Elaina O'Mahoney

entities.name: LLM
entities.how_described: 本集说现在每个人都在跟自己选择的 LLM 对话，这非常孤独且不是视觉化的

evidence.quote: Yeah, what's interesting is visual collaboration is actually absent in the AI era. We are all in our tools, all by ourselves, with words or voice. I don't know if you dictate to yourself too often or speak to your LLM of choice often. I probably do that more than type these days, but it's very lonely and it's not visual. And when I go to collaborate with my coworkers, I'm now sharing words in a doc, rather than understanding through visual collaboration and designing something more easily digestible to get to decision-making faster.
evidence.speaker: Elaina O'Mahoney

evidence.quote: Now you're bringing up the point on multiplayer, and we've been talking about this for a long time. At the beginning it was more of an idea. Everybody who's used AI in one shape or form realizes that at some point you get stuck, and you're not able to fully collaborate on the same context. With a visual collaboration tool, on paper, you should be able to truly collaborate better and get stuff done in a way that you can't when you're just using an LLM of choice on the side. But for some reason I don't see enough of those use cases yet. I see a lot of people still using visual collaboration tools, PowerPoints, or Google Docs in the same way as putting comments on the side. So I'd love to know what real visual collaboration looks like for a product team that's trying to build together.
evidence.speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia

entities.name: SaaS
entities.how_described: 本集说 Mural 的定价模式反映了传统 SaaS 按座位收费的方式

evidence.quote: Yes. And I see that the same way as in the past, a lot of these SaaS companies were trying to replace the spreadsheet. They'd position themselves in the middle and say, "And you can integrate with everybody else." So I'm curious to know what the real competitive landscape is for you, and how you're thinking about integrations with other players.
evidence.speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia

evidence.quote: This is the thing that actually keeps me up at night. I wonder how many organizations that are, to use the very vibe name, "AI-native." We weren't born when tokens and LLMs were there. So our pricing model reflects a lot of the seat-based pricing that everybody now attaches to legacy SaaS. But there's almost a double-edged sword with usage. When we speak to some of our larger customers, there's almost a black market for tokens. If they use their own tokens, they'll have to go to three other employees to say, "I've got 80% of the way there with my prototype, and my tokens got cut off. Susie, can I siphon some of your tokens?" And now it disincentivizes the wrong behavior. So it's a decision we're taking with the utmost care. It goes back to the fact that we serve totally different types of businesses, from a person who just bought us for themselves, for their three-person company or even their solo consulting gig, all the way up to a Fortune 500 company with 10,000 people. We have to think of pricing models throughout that same range, and maybe the pricing models are completely different. We know the value of our product in this very near future has to be filled with AI at its core, but we also don't want to disincentivize folks from using it and have to keep an accounting ledger of tokens. Making Sure Usage Drives the Right Outcomes
evidence.speaker: Elaina O'Mahoney
